video_title: Why Are Regular People Selling BTC to Wall Street?
gist: River CEO Alex Leishman tells Natalie Brunell that retail is net-selling Bitcoin to institutions (Q2: -78,000 BTC individuals vs +115,000 BTC businesses) even as River's own client base keeps net-buying through a bear market he thinks may have more downside left; he also details River's new quantum-ready multi-sig custody system, a 'skinny Fed account' banking proposal in DC, and why River has no plans to go public.

insights.claim: In Q2, individual Bitcoin holders were net sellers of about 78,000 BTC while businesses/institutions were net buyers of about 115,000 BTC, based on River's ownership-tracking research.
insights.speaker: host, citing River's Q2 ownership report
insights.so_what: Confirms a real, measurable transfer of Bitcoin supply from individuals to institutions each quarter, not just anecdotal sentiment.
insights.quote: In Q2, -78,000 for individuals plus 115,000 for businesses.

insights.claim: Over the last decade Bitcoin ownership has shifted from being almost entirely held by individuals to accelerating institutional ownership, driven by Bitcoin's fixed supply meaning most new institutional buying must come from existing (often early/retail) holders selling.
insights.speaker: Alex Leishman
insights.so_what: As new issuance shrinks, institutional accumulation mechanically depends on retail/early-holder distribution, a structural (not cyclical) trend to track via ownership charts.
insights.quote: especially in the last few years has started to the institutional ownership has started to accelerate because there's a fixed supply of Bitcoin

insights.claim: Leishman is not worried by rising institutional Bitcoin ownership because the institutions that have bought in understand that Bitcoin's success depends on it staying decentralized, and turning it into 'Wall Street coin' would undercut their own investment.
insights.speaker: Alex Leishman
insights.so_what: Pushes back on the popular 'institutions will capture and corrupt Bitcoin' fear that has driven negative sentiment toward ETF issuers and large holders.
insights.quote: They know that if they try and make Bitcoin Wall Street coin, that actually is counterproductive to what they want to.

insights.claim: Growing institutional ownership raises an open governance question for Bitcoin: unlike before, proposals to soft-fork or hard-fork the network can now be backed by large pools of institutional capital rather than purely individual/human political capital.
insights.speaker: Alex Leishman
insights.so_what: Bitcoin's informal governance process is untested against concentrated institutional influence, a tail risk worth monitoring around future protocol-change debates.

themes.theme: Bear Market Positioning and Client Flows

insights.claim: In the last quarter -- described as the worst quarter for Bitcoin's price in a number of years -- the vast majority of River's clients did not sell any Bitcoin, and the client base overall was still a net buyer.
insights.speaker: Alex Leishman
insights.so_what: Direct evidence that a real Bitcoin-holder cohort is holding through drawdowns rather than capitulating, a bullish behavioral signal distinct from price action.
insights.quote: the vast majority of clients not sell any Bitcoin

insights.claim: The current Bitcoin bear-market drawdown of roughly 50-something percent is much shallower than prior cycles: -93% (2011), -87% (2013-2015), -84% (2017-2018), and -77% (2021-2022).
insights.speaker: host, citing River's chart
insights.so_what: A shallower drawdown than history could mean either the asset is maturing (less volatile) or that the drawdown isn't finished yet.

insights.claim: Leishman thinks there may still be more downside since the current bear market is only about nine months old while previous Bitcoin bear markets lasted a year or more, though he stresses nobody can reliably predict the bottom.
insights.speaker: Alex Leishman
insights.so_what: Tempers bottom-calling: positions sized for a bear market that could still run several more months based on historical duration.
insights.quote: Anyone pretending to know doesn't. I've been in this industry a very long time and I've never seen anyone being able to reliably predict any of this stuff.

insights.claim: River deliberately plans its finances assuming prolonged, multi-year bear markets, describing its business as seasonal without knowing when the next 'summer' will arrive.
insights.speaker: Alex Leishman
insights.so_what: A useful operating template for any Bitcoin-linked business: budget for worst-case bear-market duration rather than the most recent cycle's length.
insights.quote: we run a seasonal business, but we don't know when summer is

insights.claim: River sees a large volume of client 'target buy' orders clustered around $50,000 and $40,000, and currently has more target buy orders than target sell orders even for prices back around $100,000+.
insights.speaker: Alex Leishman
insights.so_what: Standing limit-buy demand at lower prices suggests latent dip-buying support rather than panic selling if price falls further.
insights.quote: There are a lot of target buys.

insights.claim: Leishman attributes this cycle's weak performance in crypto outside of Bitcoin primarily to capital rotating into AI investments, which he judges a bigger drag than the rise of prediction markets and sports betting.
insights.speaker: Alex Leishman
insights.so_what: If AI capital rotation is the dominant driver of altcoin weakness, altcoin performance may stay muted independent of Bitcoin's own price action as long as AI remains the preferred speculative destination.
insights.quote: I do think the AI capital rotation was probably a bigger impact than the the gambling.

insights.claim: Speculative capital that used to flow into altcoin 'gambling' has migrated to newly democratized, CFTC-regulated prediction markets, sports betting, and high-leverage perpetuals venues like Hyperliquid, reducing demand for meme coins and small-cap crypto.
insights.speaker: Alex Leishman
insights.so_what: Structural competition for speculative dollars from regulated prediction markets and leveraged perps is a headwind for altcoin trading volumes going forward.
insights.quote: crypto is kind of, you know, the toy no one wants to play with anymore

themes.theme: River's Self-Custody Philosophy and Force Field

insights.claim: Only about 15% of River's customers move their Bitcoin to self-custody; the vast majority keep it held with River.
insights.speaker: Alex Leishman
insights.so_what: Shows the real-world self-custody rate among a mainstream-leaning Bitcoin customer base is low, useful context against the common self-custody-first narrative.
insights.quote: About 15%.

insights.claim: Leishman argues most people rationally prefer delegating Bitcoin custody to a trusted institution the same way people eat at restaurants instead of cooking every meal, even though self-custody is straightforward for enthusiasts who invest time in it.
insights.speaker: Alex Leishman
insights.so_what: Reframes the self-custody debate as a convenience/trust trade-off rather than a security absolute, relevant to how custodial platforms should be designed and marketed.
insights.quote: that's like a chef saying you have to cook all of your own meals cuz, you know, it's easy for me

insights.claim: River's 'Force Field' feature lets a customer cap how much Bitcoin can be withdrawn per week and imposes a mandatory 5-day delay to raise that cap, functioning as a built-in circuit breaker that has already saved clients from social-engineering scams.
insights.speaker: Alex Leishman
insights.so_what: A time-delay withdrawal limit is a concrete, replicable security control other custodians or self-custodians could adopt against real-time scam pressure.
insights.quote: worst case, they can get out of, you know, a little bit of money in a week, but you have 5 days to react to anything happening

insights.claim: River is migrating to a new custody system in the coming months and predicts the Bitcoin developer ecosystem will eventually align on a new quantum-secure signature type, which River plans to layer on top of its existing security rules rather than replace them.
insights.speaker: Alex Leishman
insights.so_what: Signals that quantum-resistant Bitcoin signatures are viewed by an industry insider as a coming, additive protocol change worth watching for in future soft-fork proposals.
insights.quote: What I think I see, what I predict happening is Bit- Bitcoin the Bitcoin developer ecosystem will align on a new quantum-secure signature type for Bitcoin.

insights.claim: River custodies client Bitcoin in a geographically distributed multi-sig cold-storage system engineered to survive a scenario in which half of the United States goes offline, treating operational loss (not just theft) as the bigger long-run custody risk.
insights.speaker: Alex Leishman
insights.so_what: Illustrates the extreme-tail-risk design bar institutional custodians are building to, a differentiator when evaluating where to hold Bitcoin at scale.
insights.quote: we actually design um our system to survive like half of the United States going offline

themes.theme: Data Breaches and Physical Security Threats

insights.claim: Even though River itself has never had a data breach, breaches at other exchanges such as Coinbase still harm River clients because attackers cross-reference leaked customer data and impersonate 'River support' to run social-engineering and malware scams.
insights.speaker: Alex Leishman
insights.so_what: Bitcoin holders are exposed to breach risk industry-wide, not just at the platform they personally use, which should inform personal security hygiene regardless of custodian choice.

insights.claim: River has shifted to proactively taking down phishing domains as scammers set them up, describing exchange security as an ongoing 'cat and mouse game' against impersonation attacks.
insights.speaker: Alex Leishman
insights.so_what: Offensive domain takedowns are becoming a standard defensive practice among Bitcoin custodians, a service-quality differentiator to look for.
insights.quote: it's a cat and mouse game

insights.claim: Physical 'wrench attacks' against Bitcoin holders are rising, with 2026 on track to be the worst year on record and France/Paris flagged as a particular hotspot.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Rising physical-coercion risk strengthens the case for custodial or delayed-withdrawal solutions (like Force Field) over visibly self-custodied holdings for some individuals.
insights.quote: 2026 is on track for being the worst year for wrench attacks and oddly like France or Paris is the worst

insights.claim: Recommended personal security practice: keep your digital footprint small by not signing up for exchanges/services unnecessarily, treat every unsolicited email or phone call as malicious, and never engage inbound contact -- instead independently log into the official app or call the company's published number.
insights.speaker: Alex Leishman
insights.so_what: A concrete, actionable checklist investors can apply immediately to reduce social-engineering exposure across any exchange or custodian.
insights.quote: consider like your phone or email at this point in this the open sort of low trust world in of the internet, like just completely compromised

themes.theme: Fed Charter and Banking-Rail Access for Bitcoin Fintechs

insights.claim: Regulators in DC are discussing a 'skinny account' or 'payments account' Fed account type that would not earn interest and would cap overnight cash balances, letting fintechs like River get a routing number and direct payments-system access without needing a fractional-reserve bank as an intermediary.
insights.speaker: Alex Leishman
insights.so_what: If enacted, this would let Bitcoin-native fintechs bypass correspondent-bank dependency for wires/payments, a structural de-risking of the industry's banking-access problem.
insights.quote: why should the payments system, access to the payment system of the USB coupled to having an account at a fractional reserve bank

insights.claim: Kraken obtained a routing number as a Wyoming depository institution, but the Fed reportedly paused further access while it works out the broader 'skinny account' program; Leishman expects some clarity on this by the end of the year.
insights.speaker: Alex Leishman
insights.so_what: A near-term regulatory catalyst (year-end clarity) to watch for crypto-native banking access, which would affect Kraken, River, and similar firms' operating costs.
insights.quote: Kraken got something like this already.

themes.theme: River's Growth Strategy and Staying Private

insights.claim: River has no plans to go public; Leishman's stated principle is to IPO only when it's actually important for the business, and going public now would force short-term, quarterly thinking the company can't yet afford to resist.
insights.speaker: Alex Leishman
insights.so_what: Investors and clients shouldn't expect a River IPO in the near term; the company is optimizing for long-term product control over public-market liquidity or visibility.
insights.quote: we would be guppies jumping into a big shark tank and I don't think that's the right move at this point

insights.claim: Leishman cites Epic Systems -- a multi-billion-dollar private healthcare software company founded by Judy Faulkner -- as a model for staying private, noting one of its internal '10 commandments' is reportedly 'never go public.'
insights.speaker: Alex Leishman
insights.so_what: Offers a real-world precedent that large, dominant companies can outperform without public-market pressure, informing how investors should read River's (and similarly-structured firms') growth trajectory absent public disclosures.
insights.quote: if not the first, is never go public

insights.claim: River's near-term roadmap centers on perfecting a 'dual money' banking experience -- Bitcoin as savings, dollars as the transactional/spending currency -- including a full web-app rebuild, with the longer-term mission of becoming the world's most trusted financial institution serving individuals through larger institutional clients.
insights.speaker: Alex Leishman
insights.so_what: Signals River's product direction and target market expansion (up-market into larger institutional clients) for anyone evaluating it as a banking/custody partner.

insights.claim: Leishman argues the investors happiest holding Bitcoin are the ones who bought when sentiment was worst, not when it was consensus-obvious, implying today's reportedly all-time-low sentiment is itself a contrarian signal for those convinced of Bitcoin's first-principles case.
insights.speaker: Alex Leishman
insights.so_what: A direct behavioral framework for contrarian accumulation during periods of maximum pessimism, framed by an operator with visibility into real client buy/sell flows.
insights.quote: the people who are really who are the happiest that they hold Bitcoin did not get in when everyone else is really excited about it

insights.claim: Leishman says Bitcoin's fundamentals have never been stronger even as sentiment sits near multi-year lows, attributing the disconnect to social/psychological pressure from surrounding negativity rather than any actual deterioration in the fundamentals.
insights.speaker: Alex Leishman
insights.so_what: Encourages separating price/sentiment cycles from fundamental-adoption metrics (like River's steady new-client growth) when assessing where Bitcoin actually stands.
insights.quote: I'm not sure why people are getting as bearish as they are because the fundamentals really have never been stronger, right?
